objectives.text: explain the concept of energy
discuss the inter-conversion and conservation of mass energy
examine the role of photosynthesis in the conversion of energy
analyse the transfer of energy in the environment
examine the importance of food as a source of energy
examine the process of digestion in humans
relate the structure of the teeth to their function in human digestion
evaluate the importance of respiration in providing energy to organisms
distinguish between aerobic and anaerobic respiration
examine the mechanism of breathing
explain the importance of gaseous exchange in organisms
explain the effects of smoking on the gaseous exchange process

topics.title: Fossil Fuels and Alternative Sources of Energy

objectives.text: examine the use of fossil fuels
appraise the extent to which alternative sources of energy can be used in the Caribbean
examine the use of conductors of electricity
examine the flow of electricity in circuits
assess the consumption of electricity in the home
discuss the safety features of electrical devices
discuss energy conservation measures
compare artificial sources of light
discuss first aid methods for treating electrical accidents
discuss the hazards associated with electricity
discuss the various methods of extinguishing fires
explain the appropriate use of conventional protective gear/wear
examine the application of the methods of heat transfer
outline the use of thermostats in household appliances
compare the types of thermometers
explain temperature regulation in humans
explain the need for proper ventilation

objective.text: explain the concept of energy

paper01.stem: The SI unit of energy is the
paper01.explanation: Energy (and work) is measured in joules (J).

objective.text: explain the concept of energy

paper01.stem: Energy stored in food, fuels and batteries is called
paper01.explanation: Food, fuels and batteries store chemical (potential) energy.

objective.text: explain the concept of energy

paper01.stem: A stretched rubber band has
paper01.explanation: Energy stored in a stretched or compressed object is elastic (strain) potential energy.

objective.text: explain the concept of energy

paper01.stem: A coconut hanging on a tall tree has MAINLY
paper01.explanation: Its position above the ground gives it gravitational potential energy.

objective.text: explain the concept of energy

paper01.stem: Which of the following objects possesses kinetic energy?

options.A: A book resting on a shelf

paper01.explanation: Kinetic energy is the energy of movement.

objective.text: explain the concept of energy

paper01.stem: Which of the following is a form of energy?
paper01.explanation: Sound, light, heat, kinetic, potential, chemical, electrical and nuclear are forms of energy.

objective.text: explain the concept of energy

paper01.stem: A battery in a toy car stores energy in the form of
paper01.explanation: The battery stores chemical energy that becomes electrical energy.

objective.text: explain the concept of energy

paper01.stem: Which of the following is a renewable source of energy?
paper01.explanation: Wind is replaced naturally and will not run out.

objective.text: explain the concept of energy

paper01.stem: A boy on a bicycle at the top of a hill has the MOST
paper01.explanation: At the top he is at the greatest height; as he rolls down this becomes kinetic energy.

objective.text: explain the concept of energy

paper01.stem: One kilojoule (kJ) is equal to
paper01.explanation: Kilo means one thousand.

objective.text: explain the concept of energy

paper01.stem: Energy is BEST defined as

options.A: the force acting on a body
options.D: the mass of a body in motion

paper01.explanation: Energy is the capacity to do work.

objective.text: explain the concept of energy

paper01.stem: A book resting on a high shelf possesses
paper01.explanation: It has energy because of its raised position.

objective.text: explain the concept of energy

paper01.stem: Which of the following is an example of chemical energy?
paper01.explanation: Energy stored in the bonds of chemicals.

objective.text: explain the concept of energy

paper01.stem: Which of the following objects possesses BOTH kinetic and potential energy?

options.A: A plane flying high above the ground
options.B: A car parked at the foot of a hill
options.C: A stone resting on a table

paper01.explanation: It is moving and is at a height.

objective.text: explain the concept of energy

paper01.stem: Work is done when

options.A: a force is applied to a wall that does not move

paper01.explanation: Work = force × distance moved in the direction of the force.

objective.text: discuss the inter-conversion and conservation of mass energy

paper01.stem: The law of conservation of energy states that energy

options.A: can be created but not destroyed
options.B: is always lost when it is converted
options.D: can neither be created nor destroyed but can be changed from one form to another

paper01.explanation: Energy is conserved: the total stays the same, it only changes form.

objective.text: discuss the inter-conversion and conservation of mass energy

paper01.stem: Which of the following energy conversions takes place in an electric fan?
paper01.explanation: The fan's motor converts electrical energy into kinetic (and some heat and sound) energy.

objective.text: discuss the inter-conversion and conservation of mass energy

paper01.stem: The main energy conversion in a torch (flashlight) is
paper01.explanation: Chemical energy in the cells becomes electrical energy and then light (and heat) in the bulb.

objective.text: discuss the inter-conversion and conservation of mass energy

paper01.stem: The energy of the sun is produced by
paper01.explanation: In the sun, hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium, converting mass into energy.

objective.text: discuss the inter-conversion and conservation of mass energy

paper01.stem: In a nuclear power station, energy is released when uranium atoms split. This process is called
paper01.explanation: Nuclear fission is the splitting of heavy nuclei such as uranium.

objective.text: discuss the inter-conversion and conservation of mass energy

paper01.stem: When a car brakes to a stop, its kinetic energy is converted MAINLY into
paper01.explanation: Friction in the brakes converts kinetic energy to heat.

objective.text: discuss the inter-conversion and conservation of mass energy

paper01.stem: Which of the following would help a motorist to REDUCE fuel consumption?

options.A: Carrying heavy loads in the trunk at all times
options.C: Leaving the engine idling while parked

paper01.explanation: Under-inflated tyres increase rolling resistance; correct pressure saves fuel.

objective.text: discuss the inter-conversion and conservation of mass energy

paper01.stem: Which of the following gases in vehicle exhaust is poisonous because it combines with haemoglobin?
paper01.explanation: Carbon monoxide combines with haemoglobin and reduces the oxygen carried by the blood.

objective.text: discuss the inter-conversion and conservation of mass energy

paper01.stem: A catalytic converter is fitted to the exhaust of a car in order to

options.A: change harmful gases into less harmful gases
options.B: increase the speed of the car
options.D: increase the amount of carbon monoxide produced

paper01.explanation: It converts carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides and unburnt fuel into CO₂, N₂ and water.

objective.text: discuss the inter-conversion and conservation of mass energy

paper01.stem: Which of the following energy conversions takes place when a match is struck?
paper01.explanation: Chemicals in the match head react and release heat and light.

paper01.stem: A filament lamp is supplied with 100 J of electrical energy and gives out 10 J of light energy. How much energy is wasted as heat?
paper01.explanation: Energy is conserved: 100 J - 10 J = 90 J is lost as heat.

objective.text: discuss the inter-conversion and conservation of mass energy

paper01.stem: The efficiency of the lamp described above is
paper01.explanation: Efficiency = useful output ÷ input × 100 = 10 ÷ 100 × 100 = 10%.

objective.text: discuss the inter-conversion and conservation of mass energy

paper01.stem: Which of the following energy changes occurs in a loudspeaker?
paper01.explanation: A loudspeaker changes electrical signals into sound; a microphone does the reverse.

objective.text: discuss the inter-conversion and conservation of mass energy

paper01.stem: In a car engine, the energy stored in gasoline is changed MAINLY into
paper01.explanation: Most of the chemical energy becomes heat; some becomes kinetic energy of the car.

objective.text: discuss the inter-conversion and conservation of mass energy

paper01.stem: Which of the following is an effect of internal combustion engines on the environment?

options.B: Air pollution by carbon monoxide and nitrogen oxides

paper01.explanation: Burning fuel releases harmful gases and CO₂.

objective.text: discuss the inter-conversion and conservation of mass energy

paper01.stem: Which of the following would REDUCE the harmful effects of vehicles on the environment?
paper01.explanation: Fewer vehicles on the road means less fuel burnt.

objective.text: discuss the inter-conversion and conservation of mass energy

paper01.stem: Electric and hybrid cars help to reduce pollution in cities because they

options.A: produce little or no exhaust gases while driving

paper01.explanation: Electric motors produce no exhaust at the point of use.

objective.text: examine the role of photosynthesis in the conversion of energy

paper01.stem: Which of the following is the word equation for photosynthesis?

options.A: Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy
options.C: Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen (in light, with chlorophyll)

paper01.explanation: Photosynthesis: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen, using light energy absorbed by chlorophyll.

objective.text: examine the role of photosynthesis in the conversion of energy

paper01.stem: The balanced chemical equation for photosynthesis is
paper01.explanation: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ (light and chlorophyll are needed).

objective.text: examine the role of photosynthesis in the conversion of energy

paper01.stem: During photosynthesis, light energy is converted into
paper01.explanation: Light energy is stored as chemical energy in glucose.

objective.text: examine the role of photosynthesis in the conversion of energy

paper01.stem: The pigment which absorbs light for photosynthesis is
paper01.explanation: Chlorophyll, in chloroplasts, absorbs light energy.

objective.text: examine the role of photosynthesis in the conversion of energy

paper01.stem: The chemical used to test a leaf for the presence of starch is

objective.text: examine the role of photosynthesis in the conversion of energy

paper01.stem: Plants convert much of the glucose made in photosynthesis into starch MAINLY because starch

options.B: is insoluble and can be stored without affecting osmosis in the cells
options.D: gives the leaf its green colour

paper01.explanation: Starch is insoluble, so it can be stored in large amounts without drawing water into cells by osmosis. Glucose is also used to make cellulose and, with nitrates, proteins.

paper01.explanation: CO₂ from air and water from soil are used.

objective.text: examine the role of photosynthesis in the conversion of energy

paper01.stem: Photosynthesis takes place MAINLY in the
paper01.explanation: Leaves have most chloroplasts and are adapted to absorb light.

paper01.stem: Plants in a greenhouse grew faster when extra carbon dioxide was added to the air. This is because carbon dioxide

options.A: is a raw material for photosynthesis

paper01.explanation: More CO₂ increases the rate of photosynthesis if light and temperature are suitable.

objective.text: examine the role of photosynthesis in the conversion of energy

paper01.stem: Which of the following is NOT needed for photosynthesis?
paper01.explanation: Oxygen is a product, not a requirement.

paper01.explanation: Removing the green colour makes the iodine colour change easy to see.

paper01.explanation: Ethanol vapour catches fire easily.

paper01.stem: Which of the following shows that light energy is converted to chemical energy in photosynthesis?

options.A: Glucose is produced and stored as starch

paper01.explanation: The energy is stored in the chemical bonds of glucose.

objective.text: examine the role of photosynthesis in the conversion of energy

paper01.stem: Which of the following shows the colours observed at X and Y after the leaf was tested with iodine solution?
paper01.explanation: X received light and made starch (blue-black). Y was covered, so no photosynthesis and iodine stays brown.

objective.text: examine the role of photosynthesis in the conversion of energy

paper01.stem: This experiment shows that

options.B: carbon dioxide is needed for photosynthesis

paper01.explanation: The only difference between X and Y was light.

paper01.stem: Before the experiment, the plant was kept in the dark for 48 hours in order to

options.A: remove the starch already present in the leaves
options.D: allow the leaves to absorb more water

paper01.explanation: Destarching ensures any starch found was made during the experiment.

objective.text: examine the role of photosynthesis in the conversion of energy

paper01.stem: Above a light intensity of about 6 units the rate of photosynthesis stops increasing. The MOST likely reason is that

options.B: light is not needed any more
options.C: the plant is respiring too fast
options.D: another factor such as carbon dioxide or temperature is limiting the rate

paper01.explanation: Once light is plentiful, another factor becomes limiting.

paper01.explanation: Arrows point from the organism eaten to the one that eats it, showing the flow of energy.

paper01.explanation: Decomposers recycle nutrients from dead matter.

paper01.explanation: A community is all the populations of different species in an area; a population is one species.

paper01.explanation: Much energy is used in respiration and lost as heat; some is in parts not eaten or in faeces.

paper01.stem: A pyramid of numbers for the food chain mango tree → caterpillars → birds would be

options.A: wider at the top than the bottom
options.B: narrow at the base and wide in the middle
options.C: the same width at every level
options.D: wide at the base and narrow at the top

paper01.explanation: One large tree supports many caterpillars, which support fewer birds, so the base bar is narrow.

objective.text: analyse the transfer of energy in the environment

paper01.stem: Which type of ecological pyramid is ALWAYS wider at the base than at the top?
paper01.explanation: Energy is always lost at each level, so a pyramid of energy is never inverted.

paper01.explanation: Phytoplankton (microscopic algae) are the main producers in aquatic ecosystems.

paper01.explanation: Herbivores such as goats and cows eat plants.

paper01.stem: An omnivore eats
paper01.explanation: Humans and pigs are omnivores.

paper01.stem: A group of organisms of the same species living in one area is a
paper01.explanation: A population is one species; a community is many species.

paper01.stem: The place where an organism lives is its
paper01.explanation: A habitat is the natural home of an organism.

options.A: only the plants in an area
options.B: only the animals in an area
options.D: a community of organisms together with their non-living environment

paper01.explanation: Ecosystems include both living and non-living parts.

paper01.explanation: It eats the primary consumer.

paper01.explanation: Producers are trophic level 1; primary consumers are level 2.

paper01.explanation: They capture light energy by photosynthesis.

paper01.explanation: Fewer predators means more prey survive; this upsets ecological balance.

options.B: Much energy is lost at each trophic level so little is available to them

objective.text: analyse the transfer of energy in the environment

paper01.explanation: Less grazing lets phytoplankton increase; less food means fewer small fish.

paper01.explanation: Caterpillars and grasshoppers feed directly on the producers.

paper01.stem: Which organism is a tertiary consumer in the food chain grass → caterpillar → frog → snake?
paper01.explanation: Grass is the producer, caterpillar primary, frog secondary and snake tertiary consumer.

paper01.explanation: Frogs are the snakes' only food in this web, so snakes would decrease.

paper01.explanation: Staples are starchy foods such as cereals and ground provisions.

objective.text: discuss the safety features of electrical devices

paper01.stem: The fuse in a plug is connected to the live wire so that

options.B: the appliance is disconnected from the high voltage if the fuse melts
options.D: the neutral wire carries more current

paper01.explanation: When the fuse blows, the live connection is broken so the appliance is no longer at a dangerous voltage.

objective.text: discuss the safety features of electrical devices

paper01.stem: A 690 W blender is used on a 230 V supply. Which fuse should be fitted in its plug?
paper01.explanation: I = P ÷ V = 690 ÷ 230 = 3 A. The fuse must be rated slightly ABOVE the normal current, so a 5 A fuse is used; 13 A would not protect the appliance.

objective.text: discuss the safety features of electrical devices

paper01.stem: Plugging too many appliances into one socket is dangerous because

options.D: the large current may overheat the wires and cause a fire

paper01.explanation: Overloading draws a large current which heats the wires and can melt insulation.

objective.text: discuss the safety features of electrical devices

paper01.stem: Thick cables are used for heavy-duty appliances such as electric stoves because thick wires

options.C: have less resistance and do not overheat

paper01.explanation: Thicker wires have lower resistance, so large currents produce less heat.

objective.text: discuss the safety features of electrical devices

paper01.stem: The earth wire in an appliance with a metal case

options.B: provides a safe path for current if the case becomes live
options.C: controls the speed of the appliance

paper01.explanation: If a fault makes the case live, current flows to earth, the fuse blows and the user is protected.

paper01.explanation: Blue = neutral, brown = live, green/yellow = earth.

paper01.explanation: Excess current heats and melts the fuse wire.

paper01.explanation: I = 3 000 ÷ 240 = 12.5 A, so a 13 A fuse is needed.

paper01.explanation: Damaged insulation exposes conductors.

objective.text: discuss first aid methods for treating electrical accidents

paper01.stem: A person is receiving an electric shock from a faulty appliance. The FIRST thing a rescuer should do is to

options.B: switch off the power at the mains

paper01.explanation: Touching the person would pass current to the rescuer; the supply must be cut first.

paper01.stem: If the power cannot be switched off, the rescuer should separate the casualty from the source using
paper01.explanation: Dry wood is an insulator.

paper01.stem: A minor burn should be treated by

options.C: cooling it under clean running water

paper01.explanation: Cool running water for about 20 minutes reduces damage and pain; then cover with a clean, non-fluffy dressing.

objective.text: discuss first aid methods for treating electrical accidents

paper01.stem: A person has a burn on the hand from touching a hot iron. The FIRST treatment should be to

options.B: hold the burn under cool running water

paper01.explanation: Cooling reduces tissue damage and pain.

objective.text: discuss first aid methods for treating electrical accidents

paper01.stem: After a casualty of electric shock has been separated from the supply, the rescuer should check for
paper01.explanation: If there is no breathing, CPR should begin.

objective.text: discuss first aid methods for treating electrical accidents

paper01.stem: An electrical burn can be more serious than it appears because

options.B: the current may damage tissues deep inside the body

paper01.explanation: Current passing through the body can damage internal organs.

objective.text: discuss first aid methods for treating electrical accidents

paper01.stem: The FIRST thing to do when a person receives an electric shock and is still in contact with the wire is to

options.A: switch off the power at the main switch
options.B: pull the person away with bare hands

paper01.explanation: Rescuers must not become part of the circuit.

objective.text: discuss first aid methods for treating electrical accidents

paper01.stem: If the power cannot be switched off, the victim of an electric shock should be moved away from the wire using
paper01.explanation: Dry wood is an insulator.

objective.text: discuss first aid methods for treating electrical accidents

paper01.stem: An electric shock victim is not breathing and has no pulse. The first-aider should

options.B: call for help and begin CPR

paper01.explanation: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation keeps blood and oxygen moving.

objective.text: discuss first aid methods for treating electrical accidents

paper01.stem: A minor electrical burn on the hand should be

options.C: cooled under running water and covered with a clean dressing

paper01.explanation: Cooling reduces tissue damage; dressing prevents infection.

objective.text: discuss first aid methods for treating electrical accidents

paper01.stem: An unconscious victim who is breathing should be placed in the
paper01.explanation: It keeps the airway open.

objective.text: discuss first aid methods for treating electrical accidents

paper01.stem: A person who has received an electric shock should be kept warm and calm and should

options.D: be checked by a doctor even if they seem fine

paper01.explanation: Shock can affect the heart rhythm some time later.

objective.text: discuss the hazards associated with electricity

options.A: the kite string may conduct electricity if it touches the lines
options.B: the wind is stronger near power lines
options.C: the kite will be burnt by the sun

paper01.explanation: A damp or wire-reinforced string can carry current from the line to the person.

paper01.stem: Illegal connections to electricity lines are dangerous MAINLY because they

options.D: increase the voltage in the home

paper01.explanation: Unsafe wiring without fuses and insulation can cause shocks and fires.

paper01.stem: The back of a television should NOT be removed by an untrained person, even when it is switched off, because

options.D: some parts store electric charge and can give a shock

paper01.explanation: Capacitors inside can hold a dangerous charge after the set is unplugged.

paper01.stem: Which of the following should NOT be placed in a microwave oven?
paper01.explanation: Metal reflects microwaves and can cause sparks and fires.

paper01.explanation: Metal conducts; contact with lines can be fatal.

options.D: water conducts electricity and increases the risk of shock

paper01.explanation: Wet skin lowers resistance, allowing more current through the body.

options.A: protect it from sudden increases in voltage

paper01.explanation: Power surges can damage electronic components.

paper01.stem: Which of the following is an electrical hazard in the home?
paper01.explanation: All three can cause shocks or fires.

options.B: water conducts electricity and could cause a shock
options.D: the dryer uses too little current

paper01.explanation: Water provides a path for current through the body.

objective.text: discuss the hazards associated with electricity

paper01.stem: During a thunderstorm it is safest to

options.D: stay indoors away from electrical appliances

paper01.explanation: Lightning strikes tall objects and open ground.

objective.text: discuss the hazards associated with electricity

paper01.stem: Which of the following should NOT be done when changing a light bulb?
paper01.explanation: The lamp holder may be live.

parts.context: Nadia placed a potted plant in a dark cupboard for 48 hours. She then covered part of one leaf on both sides with aluminium foil, as shown in Figure 1, and placed the plant in sunlight for six hours. The leaf was then removed and tested for starch.

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Explain why the plant was kept in a dark cupboard for 48 hours before the experiment.

points: To destarch the leaves / remove starch already present (1)
so that any starch found at the end must have been made during the experiment (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: State the colour you would expect at X and at Y after the leaf is tested with iodine solution.

points: X - blue-black (1)
Y - brown/orange-brown (1)

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: State the conclusion that can be drawn from this experiment.

points: Light is needed for photosynthesis (for starch to be made).

items.label: (iv)
items.prompt: Outline the steps used to test a leaf for starch. You MUST include ONE safety precaution.

points: Boil the leaf in water for about 1 minute to kill it / break down cell membranes (1)
Place the leaf in hot ethanol (in a water bath) to remove the chlorophyll (1)
Dip in hot water to soften, spread on a white tile and add iodine solution (1)
Precaution: turn off the flame before heating ethanol / heat ethanol in a water bath because it is flammable (1)

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Write a balanced chemical equation for photosynthesis.

points: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ (light, chlorophyll)
markScheme.guidance: 1 mark for correct reactants and products; 1 mark for balancing

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Explain why photosynthesis is important to animals.

points: It converts light energy into chemical energy in food (glucose) (1)
which is passed to animals through food chains - animals depend directly or indirectly on plants for food (1)
it releases oxygen which animals need for respiration (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

parts.label: (c)
parts.context: Figure 2 shows a simple food web in a pond.

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Name the producer in the food web.

points: Algae

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Write out ONE food chain from Figure 2 that contains FOUR organisms.

points: Algae → tadpole → large fish → heron
OR Algae → water flea → large fish → heron

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: Explain why food chains rarely have more than five trophic levels.

points: Energy is lost at each trophic level (as heat in respiration, movement, undigested waste) (1)
so too little energy remains to support organisms at higher levels (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (iv)
items.prompt: Predict what would happen to the number of water fleas if all the large fish were removed. Give a reason.

points: Water fleas would increase (1)
because they would no longer be eaten by large fish (1) (accept: may later decrease when algae run out)
markScheme.guidance: 1 mark for prediction; 1 mark for reason

parts.label: (a)
parts.context: Table 1 shows the nutrients found in some foods eaten by a student in one day.

table.title: TABLE 1: FOODS EATEN BY A STUDENT

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Define the term 'balanced diet'.

points: A diet which contains all the nutrients (and water and fibre) in the correct proportions for a person's needs.

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: State the function of EACH of the following in the body: protein; vitamin C; fibre.

points: Protein - growth and repair of tissues (1)
Vitamin C - healthy gums/skin, healing of wounds, prevents scurvy (1)
Fibre - adds bulk, helps peristalsis, prevents constipation (1)

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: Explain why a construction worker needs more carbohydrates each day than an office clerk of the same age and sex.

points: The construction worker is more physically active / does heavy manual work (1)
so he uses more energy, which is supplied mainly by carbohydrates (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Identify the organs labelled B, C and E.

points: B - liver
C - stomach
E - small intestine

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Explain the role of bile in the digestion of fats.

points: Bile (made in the liver, stored in the gall bladder) emulsifies fats (1)
breaking large fat globules into tiny droplets, increasing the surface area (1)
so that lipase can digest the fats faster into fatty acids and glycerol (1) (bile also neutralises stomach acid)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Distinguish between 'absorption' and 'assimilation'.

points: Absorption is the movement of digested food through the wall of the small intestine (villi) into the blood/lymph (1)
assimilation is the use of absorbed food by body cells, e.g. amino acids to make proteins (1)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Name ONE food additive and state ONE effect it may have on health.

points: e.g. salt - high blood pressure; MSG - headaches; artificial colouring - allergies/hyperactivity; artificial sweetener - digestive upset
markScheme.guidance: 1 mark for additive with matching effect

parts.label: (a)
parts.context: Students investigated the effect of temperature on the digestion of starch by amylase. They mixed equal volumes of starch solution and amylase at different temperatures and recorded the time taken for the starch to disappear (iodine no longer turned blue-black). Their results are shown in Table 2.

table.title: TABLE 2: TIME TAKEN FOR STARCH TO BE DIGESTED

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: The rate of reaction can be calculated as 1 ÷ time. Calculate the rate of reaction at 20 °C and at 40 °C. Show your working.

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: On the grid provided, plot a graph of time taken against temperature for the temperatures from 10 °C to 50 °C. You MUST label EACH axis.

points: Axes labelled with units
Suitable scale
Smooth curve
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for correct plotting of points (all points = 2; at least half = 1); 1 mark for both axes labelled with units; 1 mark for an appropriate scale (at least 75% of the grid used); 1 mark for a smooth line/curve joining the points

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: Using the results, state the optimum temperature for amylase in this experiment.

points: About 40 °C

items.label: (iv)
items.prompt: Explain why the starch was NOT digested at 60 °C.

points: The high temperature denatured the enzyme (1)
changing the shape of its active site so starch could no longer fit/bind (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (v)
items.prompt: State TWO variables which the students should have kept constant.

points: Volume/concentration of starch solution
Volume/concentration of amylase
pH
Number of drops of iodine / interval between tests

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Define the term 'enzyme'.

points: A protein that acts as a biological catalyst, speeding up chemical reactions in living organisms (by lowering the activation energy).

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Complete Table 3 by stating the substrate and product of EACH enzyme.

points: Pepsin: protein → polypeptides (1 + 1)
Lipase: fats → fatty acids and glycerol (1 + 1)
markScheme.guidance: 1 mark each for substrate and product

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: Suggest why pepsin stops working when it passes from the stomach into the duodenum.

points: Pepsin works best in acidic conditions (low pH) in the stomach (1)
the duodenum is alkaline because bile/pancreatic juice neutralises the acid (1)
the change in pH alters the shape of the enzyme so it no longer works (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Identify the parts labelled P, Q and R.

points: P - enamel
Q - dentine
R - pulp cavity

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Explain how eating sugary snacks between meals may lead to tooth decay.

points: Bacteria in plaque feed on the sugar (1)
and produce acids (1)
which dissolve the enamel and dentine, forming cavities (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: State TWO ways of caring for the teeth.

points: Brush at least twice a day (with fluoride toothpaste)
Floss daily
Reduce sugary foods and drinks
Visit the dentist regularly
Rinse with mouthwash

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Write the word equation for aerobic respiration.

points: Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy
markScheme.guidance: 1 mark for reactants; 1 mark for products

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: State TWO differences between aerobic and anaerobic respiration in humans.

points: Aerobic uses oxygen; anaerobic does not
Aerobic releases much more energy
Aerobic produces carbon dioxide and water; anaerobic produces lactic acid

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: Explain why a sprinter's leg muscles may ache after a 100 m race.

points: During the race the muscles need energy faster than oxygen can be supplied (1)
so they respire anaerobically (1)
producing lactic acid which builds up and causes fatigue/cramp (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: State the observation you would expect in the limewater connected to flask A and to flask B after 24 hours.

points: A - limewater turns milky/cloudy (1)
B - limewater stays clear (1)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Explain why flask B was included in the experiment.

points: It is a control (1)
boiled seeds are dead and cannot respire, so it shows that the carbon dioxide came from living (respiring) seeds (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: State ONE source of error in this experiment and suggest how it could be reduced.

points: Bacteria/fungi on the boiled seeds may respire - soak seeds in disinfectant (1 + 1)
Air leaks at the bungs - seal joints with Vaseline (1 + 1)
Carbon dioxide from the air in the flask - use a flask with CO₂ absorbed / fill quickly (1 + 1)
markScheme.guidance: 1 mark for error; 1 mark for matching improvement

parts.context: Figure 6 shows a bell jar model of the chest.

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Describe the steps Marlon should take to help his neighbour safely.

points: Switch off the power at the mains / do not touch the casualty until the power is off (1)
If the power cannot be switched off, push the casualty away using a dry wooden object while standing on dry insulating material (1)
Call for emergency help (1)
Check breathing; if not breathing begin CPR (chest compressions and rescue breaths) / treat burns with cool water (1)
markScheme.guidance: 1 mark each for any four correct steps in a logical order

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: State ONE item of protective gear an electrician should wear and explain its purpose.

points: Rubber gloves / rubber-soled boots (1) - insulate the worker from electric current (1)
Goggles (1) - protect eyes from sparks (1)
Helmet (1) - protect head from falling objects (1)
markScheme.guidance: 1 mark for item; 1 mark for purpose

parts.label: (a)
parts.context: Students carried out food tests on four local foods. Their observations are shown in Table 1.

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Using the results in Table 1, state the nutrients present in EACH food.

points: Green banana - starch
Ripe mango - reducing sugar
Ackee - protein and fat
Red peas - starch and protein

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Suggest why ripe mango contains reducing sugar while green banana contains starch.

points: During ripening starch is converted to sugars (by enzymes) (1)
so ripe fruits taste sweet while unripe fruits are starchy (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: Describe how the Benedict's test is carried out.

points: Crush/mix the food with a little water in a test tube (1)
add an equal volume of Benedict's solution (1)
heat in a boiling water bath for a few minutes and observe the colour (1)

items.label: (iv)
items.prompt: State ONE safety precaution for the Benedict's test.

points: Use a water bath instead of heating directly
Point the test tube away from people
Wear goggles

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Construct a table to show ONE food rich in EACH of the following and ONE function of the nutrient: carbohydrate, protein, fat.

points: Title (1)
Enclosed table with suitable headings (1)
Carbohydrate e.g. rice/yam - supplies energy (1)
Protein e.g. fish/peas - growth and repair (1)
Fat e.g. butter/ackee - stores energy/insulation (1)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Explain why the diet of a 16-year-old athlete should differ from that of a 70-year-old retiree.

points: The athlete is growing and very active (1)
so needs more energy (carbohydrates) and more protein for muscle growth and repair (1)
the retiree is less active, so needs fewer kilojoules to avoid obesity but enough calcium/vitamins (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Name ONE deficiency disease and the nutrient whose lack causes it.

points: Scurvy - vitamin C
Rickets - vitamin D/calcium
Anaemia - iron/vitamin B₁₂
Goitre - iodine
Kwashiorkor - protein
Night blindness - vitamin A
markScheme.guidance: 1 mark for disease; 1 mark for matching nutrient

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Identify the parts labelled P, Q and S.

points: P - trachea
Q - bronchus
S - diaphragm

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Describe the changes in the chest which cause air to enter the lungs.

points: The diaphragm contracts and flattens and the intercostal muscles contract, moving the ribs up and out (1)
the volume of the chest cavity increases (1)
so the pressure inside the lungs falls below atmospheric pressure and air rushes in (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: State TWO features of the alveoli which make them efficient for gaseous exchange.

points: Very large surface area
Walls one cell thick/thin
Moist lining
Rich blood supply (network of capillaries)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Explain why the composition of exhaled air differs from that of inhaled air.

points: Oxygen diffuses from the alveoli into the blood for respiration, so exhaled air has less oxygen (1)
carbon dioxide and water vapour from respiration diffuse into the alveoli, so exhaled air has more of them (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

parts.label: (c)
parts.context: A man collapses at a cricket match and is not breathing.

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Outline the steps a trained first-aider should take when giving cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR).

points: Check for danger and response, then call for emergency help/AED (1)
Open the airway by tilting the head back and lifting the chin; check breathing (1)
Give 30 chest compressions in the centre of the chest, about 5-6 cm deep, at 100-120 per minute (1)
Give 2 rescue breaths and continue 30:2 until help arrives or the casualty breathes (1)
markScheme.guidance: 1 mark each for any four steps in order

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Explain why CPR can keep a casualty alive until medical help arrives.

points: It keeps oxygenated blood flowing to the brain and other organs.

parts.label: (a)
parts.context: A student connected a resistor in series with an ammeter and a variable power supply. A voltmeter was connected across the resistor. The results are shown in Table 2.

table.title: TABLE 2: VOLTAGE AND CURRENT FOR A RESISTOR

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Draw a circuit diagram of the apparatus the student used.

points: Supply, resistor and ammeter in series (1)
Voltmeter in parallel across the resistor (1)
Correct symbols, lines drawn with a ruler (1)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: On the grid provided, plot a graph of current against voltage and draw the line of best fit.

points: All six points correctly plotted
Axes labelled with units
Suitable scale
Straight line through the origin
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for correct plotting of points (all points = 2; at least half = 1); 1 mark for both axes labelled with units; 1 mark for an appropriate scale (at least 75% of the grid used); 1 mark for a smooth line/curve joining the points

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: Describe the relationship between voltage and current shown by your graph.

points: Current is directly proportional to voltage (straight line through the origin).

items.label: (iv)
items.prompt: Calculate the resistance of the resistor. Show your working.

markScheme.guidance: 1 mark for correct substitution/working; 1 mark for correct answer with unit

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Calculate the power used by the resistor when the voltage is 8 V.

markScheme.guidance: 1 mark for correct substitution/working; 1 mark for correct answer with unit

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: State ONE precaution the student should take to obtain accurate readings.

points: Switch off between readings so the resistor does not heat up
Read meters at eye level
Check meters read zero before starting
Repeat readings and average

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: State the units of electrical power and electrical resistance.

points: Power - watt (W) (1)
Resistance - ohm (Ω) (1)

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Distinguish between a series circuit and a parallel circuit.

points: In a series circuit components are connected one after another in a single path, so the same current flows through each (1)
in a parallel circuit components are on separate branches, each connected across the supply (1)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Explain why Christmas lights wired in series all go out when one bulb fails.

points: There is only one path for the current (1)
so a broken filament breaks the whole circuit and no current flows (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

parts.label: (a)
parts.context: Table 3 compares three types of light bulb that give the same brightness.

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Calculate the energy used by the filament bulb over its lifetime, in kWh.

markScheme.guidance: 1 mark for correct substitution/working; 1 mark for correct answer with unit

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Calculate the energy used by the LED bulb in 1 000 hours and hence the energy saved compared with the filament bulb.

points: Saving = 60 - 9 = 51 kWh (1)

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: Although the LED bulb costs more to buy, explain why it is the most economical choice.

points: It uses much less power, so running costs are lower (1)
it lasts 25 times longer, so fewer replacements are bought (1)
over its lifetime the savings on electricity far exceed the higher purchase price (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: State TWO ways, other than changing bulbs, in which a family can conserve electrical energy.

points: Switch off lights and appliances when not in use
Unplug chargers/standby appliances
Use natural light/ventilation
Use occupancy sensors/timers
Repair faulty appliances

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Compare a fluorescent tube and a filament lamp in terms of shadow formation and similarity to daylight.

points: A fluorescent tube is an extended source and gives soft shadows, while a filament lamp is nearly a point source and gives sharp shadows (1)
fluorescent (daylight) tubes give light closer to daylight; filament light is yellowish (1)

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Explain why an overloaded extension cord may cause a fire.

points: Many appliances together draw a large current (1)
the large current heats the wires (1)
the insulation can melt/burn and set nearby materials on fire (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: State ONE hazard of flying kites near overhead power lines.

points: The string may touch the lines and conduct electricity, causing electrocution.

parts.label: (a)
parts.context: Rods of equal length and thickness made of four different materials were fixed to a metal box of hot water. A drawing pin was stuck with wax to the far end of each rod. The time taken for each pin to fall was recorded. The results are shown in Table 4.

table.title: TABLE 4: TIME FOR PINS TO FALL

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: On the grid provided, draw a bar chart of the times for copper, aluminium and iron.

points: Three bars of correct height
Axes labelled (Material; Time for pin to fall/s)
Bars of equal width and equally spaced
Suitable scale

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Arrange the materials in order from the BEST to the WORST conductor of heat.

points: Copper, aluminium, iron, glass

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: Explain how heat is conducted along a metal rod.

points: Particles at the hot end gain energy and vibrate faster (1)
they pass energy to neighbouring particles by collisions (1)
free electrons in metals move and carry energy quickly along the rod (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

items.label: (iv)
items.prompt: State TWO variables which were kept constant in this experiment.

points: Length of rods
Thickness of rods
Temperature of water
Amount of wax
Size of pins

items.label: (v)
items.prompt: Suggest ONE source of error.

points: Different amounts of wax on each pin
Reaction time in using the stopwatch
Water cooling during the experiment

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Explain how EACH of the following reduces heat loss from hot tea in the flask: the vacuum; the silvered surfaces; the stopper.

points: Vacuum: there are no particles, so heat cannot be lost by conduction (1) or convection (1)
Silvered surfaces: reflect radiant heat (1) back into the flask (1)
Stopper: prevents convection currents/evaporation (1) and is made of a poor conductor (1)

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Explain why a metal spoon left in hot soup feels hotter than a wooden spoon.

points: Metal is a good conductor of heat, wood is a poor conductor (insulator) (1)
heat is conducted quickly up the metal spoon to the handle (1)
and from the metal to the hand, so it feels hotter (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: From Figure 3, name ONE producer, ONE herbivore and ONE carnivore.

points: Producer: grass/cabbage (1)
Herbivore: caterpillar/grasshopper (1)
Carnivore: frog/snake/bird/hawk (1)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Write a food chain from the web which has FIVE organisms.

points: Grass/cabbage → caterpillar/grasshopper → frog → snake → hawk

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: The farmer sprays insecticide which kills most caterpillars and grasshoppers. Predict and explain the effect on the population of hawks.

points: The hawk population would decrease (1)
because the frogs and birds that feed on the insects would have less food and decrease (1)
so the hawks would have fewer snakes and birds to eat (the insecticide may also build up in the food chain) (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Define the term 'trophic level'.

points: The feeding position of an organism in a food chain.

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Explain why a pyramid of energy is always wider at the base than at the top.

points: Producers trap the most energy from the sun (1)
energy is lost at each level through respiration (heat), movement, excretion and uneaten parts (1)
so less energy is available to each higher trophic level (about 10% passes on) (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: State the role of decomposers in an ecosystem.

points: They break down dead organisms and waste (1)
releasing nutrients back into the soil for plants to use (1)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Distinguish between a population and a community.

points: A population is all the organisms of one species in an area (1)
a community is all the populations of different species living in an area (1)

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: On the grid provided, plot a graph of number of bubbles per minute against temperature.

points: All six points plotted
Axes labelled with units
Suitable scale
Smooth curve
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for correct plotting of points (all points = 2; at least half = 1); 1 mark for both axes labelled with units; 1 mark for an appropriate scale (at least 75% of the grid used); 1 mark for a smooth line/curve joining the points

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Use your graph to estimate the optimum temperature for fermentation.

points: About 40 °C (accept 38-42 °C).

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: Explain why no bubbles were produced at 60 °C.

points: The high temperature denatured the yeast's enzymes / killed the yeast (1)
so respiration/fermentation stopped and no carbon dioxide was produced (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (iv)
items.prompt: Name the gas given off and describe a test to identify it.

points: Carbon dioxide (1)
Bubble it through limewater, which turns milky (1)

items.label: (v)
items.prompt: Suggest ONE improvement to the method of measuring the gas produced.

points: Collect the gas in a gas syringe/measuring cylinder over water to measure volume, because bubbles vary in size.

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Write the word equation for anaerobic respiration in yeast.

points: Glucose → ethanol (alcohol) + carbon dioxide + energy
markScheme.guidance: 1 mark for ethanol + carbon dioxide; 1 mark for complete equation

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Explain how the products of anaerobic respiration by yeast are used in bakeries and breweries.

points: In bakeries, the carbon dioxide produced forms bubbles which make the dough rise (1)
the alcohol evaporates during baking (1)
in breweries the ethanol is the useful product in drinks such as beer and wine (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: State TWO differences between aerobic and anaerobic respiration.

points: Aerobic needs oxygen; anaerobic does not
Aerobic releases much more energy
Aerobic produces CO₂ and water; anaerobic produces lactic acid or ethanol and CO₂
Aerobic occurs in mitochondria; anaerobic in cytoplasm

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: State the site of aerobic respiration in a cell.

points: Mitochondria (1) in the cytoplasm of all living cells (1)

parts.label: (a)
parts.context: The Brown family is building a new house in Jamaica and wants it to stay cool without using too much electricity.

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Suggest TWO features of the house which would promote natural ventilation.

points: Windows on opposite walls (cross-ventilation)
Louvre windows
High ceilings with vents near the roof
Open verandahs/wide doors

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Explain why the roof should be painted white or a light colour.

points: Light colours reflect radiant heat from the sun (1)
so less heat is absorbed and the house stays cooler (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: Explain why a ceiling fan makes people feel cooler.

points: Moving air speeds up the evaporation of sweat from the skin (1)
evaporation takes latent heat from the body (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: The family installs an air conditioner with a thermostat. Explain how the thermostat saves energy.

points: The thermostat senses the room temperature (1)
it switches the compressor off when the set temperature is reached (1)
and on again only when the room warms up, so the unit does not run all the time (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: State TWO benefits of proper ventilation in a home.

points: Supplies fresh oxygen
Removes carbon dioxide/stale air
Removes moisture, reducing mould
Removes heat
Removes fumes/smoke

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Name the THREE methods of extinguishing a fire and give ONE example of EACH.

points: Removing heat - spraying water on burning wood (1)
Removing oxygen - fire blanket/CO₂ extinguisher/foam (1)
Removing fuel - turning off gas supply/cutting a firebreak (1)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: State ONE item of protective wear the builders should use and explain its purpose.

points: Hard hat - protects the head from falling objects (accept goggles, gloves, boots with suitable purpose).

items.prompt: On the grid provided, plot a graph of bubbles per minute against distance of the lamp.

points: Axes labelled with units
Suitable scale
Smooth curve
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for correct plotting of points (all points = 2; at least half = 1); 1 mark for both axes labelled with units; 1 mark for an appropriate scale (at least 75% of the grid used); 1 mark for a smooth line/curve joining the points

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Describe the relationship shown by your graph.

points: As the distance of the lamp increases, the number of bubbles decreases (1)
the decrease is rapid at first and then slows (not a straight line) (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: Explain the effect of moving the lamp further away on the rate of photosynthesis.

points: Moving the lamp further away reduces the light intensity reaching the plant (1)
light provides the energy for photosynthesis (1)
so the rate slows and less oxygen is produced (fewer bubbles) (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

items.label: (iv)
items.prompt: Suggest why a beaker of water was placed between the lamp and the pondweed in a repeat of this experiment.

points: To absorb heat from the lamp (1)
so that temperature is kept constant and only light intensity changes (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (v)
items.prompt: State ONE limitation of counting bubbles to measure the rate of photosynthesis.

points: Bubbles may be of different sizes
Bubbles may be too fast to count
Some oxygen dissolves in the water

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Name the gas given off and describe a test to identify it.

points: Oxygen (1)
It relights a glowing splint (1)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: State TWO factors, other than light, which affect the rate of photosynthesis.

points: Carbon dioxide concentration
Temperature
Amount of chlorophyll
Water supply

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: Explain why farmers growing tomatoes in greenhouses sometimes add carbon dioxide to the air.

points: Carbon dioxide is a raw material for photosynthesis (1)
when light and temperature are adequate, CO₂ may limit the rate (1)
adding CO₂ increases photosynthesis, so plants grow faster and yield more (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

items.prompt: Identify the structures labelled Q and R.

points: Q - blood capillary (1)
R - lacteal (1)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Describe THREE ways in which villi are adapted for the absorption of digested food.

points: Millions of villi give a very large surface area (1)
the wall is one cell thick, giving a short diffusion distance (1)
a rich blood supply/lacteal carries food away, maintaining a concentration gradient (1)

parts.label: (b)
parts.context: Table 2 shows some digestive enzymes, where they act and their substrates and products.

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Complete Table 2.

points: Salivary amylase - product: maltose
Pepsin - site: stomach
Lipase - products: fatty acids and glycerol
Trypsin - site: small intestine (duodenum)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Explain why food must be digested before it can be used by the body.

points: Large, insoluble food molecules cannot pass through the gut wall (1)
digestion breaks them into small, soluble molecules that can be absorbed into the blood (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: State the role of bile in digestion.

points: Emulsifies fats into small droplets, increasing surface area for lipase (1)
neutralises stomach acid, giving an alkaline pH for intestinal enzymes (1)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Distinguish between mechanical digestion and chemical digestion.

points: Mechanical digestion is the physical breakdown of food into smaller pieces by teeth/churning (1)
chemical digestion is the breakdown of large molecules into small ones by enzymes (1)

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: State the expected observations for the cotton wool and the limewater after five cigarettes have been smoked.

points: Cotton wool turns brown/yellow and sticky (1)
limewater turns milky (1)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Name the substance in smoke responsible for EACH observation in (a) (i).

points: Cotton wool - tar (1)
Limewater - carbon dioxide (1)

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: Explain why the cotton wool is a model of the lungs of a smoker.

points: Tar is deposited in the airways and alveoli as the smoke is breathed in (1)
just as it collects on the cotton wool, clogging the surfaces (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (iv)
items.prompt: Suggest a control for this experiment.

points: Run the machine with the same set-up but no cigarette (1)
to show that the changes are caused by the cigarette smoke and not the air (1)

parts.label: (b)
parts.context: A student wants to compare the amount of tar in two brands of cigarette.

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: State a suitable hypothesis.

points: Brand X produces more tar than Brand Y, so the cotton wool will be darker/gain more mass.
markScheme.guidance: 1 mark for a clearly stated hypothesis; 1 mark for a testable hypothesis

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Outline a method, including how the amount of tar will be measured.

points: Weigh a fresh plug of cotton wool and place it in the U-tube.
Smoke one cigarette of Brand X using the pump for a set time.
Remove and reweigh the cotton wool; record the increase in mass.
Repeat with a fresh cotton wool plug and a cigarette of Brand Y.
Repeat each three times and compare average increases in mass.
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a logical sequence (1 mark if there are flaws in the sequence); 1 mark for instructional language (command verbs); 1 mark for a method linked to the hypothesis; 1 mark for including the apparatus/materials listed

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Explain how carbon monoxide in cigarette smoke reduces the amount of oxygen carried by the blood.

points: Carbon monoxide combines with haemoglobin in red blood cells (1)
more strongly than oxygen, so less haemoglobin is available to carry oxygen (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: State TWO reasons why second-hand smoke is harmful.

points: Non-smokers breathe in tar, nicotine and carbon monoxide (1)
which increases their risk of lung disease, asthma attacks and cancer (1)
children and unborn babies are especially at risk (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

the steam produced rises and turns a turbine (1)
the turbine drives a generator which produces electricity (1)

items.label: (ii)

Switch off between readings to avoid overheating
Start at a low voltage
Check all connections are tight
Read meters at eye level

items.prompt: Draw the circuit symbols for a fuse, a voltmeter and a switch.

points: Fuse: rectangle with a line through it (1)
Voltmeter: circle containing V (1)
Switch: break with a hinged line (1)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Explain why a fuse must be connected in series in the live wire.

points: All the current must flow through the fuse so it can melt if the current is too high (1)
being in the live wire means the appliance is disconnected from the high voltage when it blows (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: A 2 kW water heater is used for 1.5 hours a day. Calculate the cost for 30 days if 1 kWh costs $0.50.

points: Energy per day = 2 × 1.5 = 3 kWh (1)
For 30 days = 90 kWh (1)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: State ONE advantage of using a solar water heater instead.

points: Uses free energy from the sun / lower electricity bills / no emissions.

parts.label: (a)
parts.context: Figure 5 shows a box-type solar cooker.

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Explain how EACH of the following features helps the cooker to work: the reflector; the black pot; the glass cover.

points: Reflector: reflects extra sunlight (1) into the box, increasing the energy received (1)
Black pot: dull black surfaces are good absorbers (1) of radiant heat (1)
Glass cover: lets radiation in (1) but traps the heated air, reducing heat loss by convection (1)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: State ONE advantage and ONE disadvantage of solar cookers.

points: Advantage: free energy / no smoke / no fuel cost / saves firewood (1)
Disadvantage: cannot be used at night or in cloudy weather / cooks slowly (1)

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Explain why the handles of pots are made of plastic or wood.

points: Plastic and wood are poor conductors (insulators) of heat (1)
so the handle stays cool enough to hold safely (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Explain how an electric fan heater warms the whole of a room by convection.

points: Air near the heater is warmed, expands and becomes less dense (1)
the warm air rises and cooler, denser air moves in to take its place (1)
a convection current circulates warm air around the room (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: State why heat from the sun can reach the earth by radiation but not by conduction or convection.

points: Space is a vacuum with no particles (1)
conduction and convection need particles, but radiation (electromagnetic waves) does not (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

Room temperature
Time intervals

keep all other conditions the same and compare temperature falls (1)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: State ONE application of insulation in the home.

points: Insulated roof/ceiling
Insulated hot water tank
Cooler/ice box
Vacuum flask
Oven gloves

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Explain how a thermostat keeps the temperature of an electric oven constant.

points: A temperature sensor/bimetallic strip responds to the oven temperature (1)
when the set temperature is reached it switches off the heating element (1)
when the oven cools below the set temperature it switches the element on again (1)

paper02.title: Food labels and a balanced diet

parts.label: (a)
parts.context: Table 6 shows part of the nutrition label on a packet of breakfast cereal.

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Calculate the energy and the carbohydrate in one 40 g serving.

points: Carbohydrate = 80 × 0.4 = 32 g (1)

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Suggest ONE reason why this cereal should be eaten only in moderation by a person with diabetes.

points: It contains a lot of sugar (30 g per 100 g) (1)
which would raise blood glucose quickly (1)
markScheme.guidance: 2 marks for a full outline; 1 mark for a partial outline

items.label: (iii)
items.prompt: State the function in the body of iron and of fibre.

points: Iron - makes haemoglobin in red blood cells (1)
Fibre - adds bulk, helps peristalsis, prevents constipation (1)

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: Explain why the energy requirement of a person depends on age, sex and occupation.

points: Growing children/teenagers need extra energy for growth (1)
males usually have more muscle and a higher metabolic rate than females (1)
people doing heavy physical work use more energy than those in sedentary jobs (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Name ONE food additive and state why it is used.

points: Salt - preservative/flavour
MSG - flavour enhancer
Artificial colouring - makes food look attractive
Artificial sweetener - sweetness without energy
markScheme.guidance: 1 mark for additive; 1 mark for use

items.label: (i)
items.prompt: State ONE symptom of kwashiorkor.

points: Swollen belly (oedema)
Thin muscles
Skin sores
Hair loss/colour change

items.label: (ii)
items.prompt: Explain why obesity increases the risk of non-communicable diseases.

points: Excess body fat is linked with high blood pressure and heart disease (1)
it makes cells less responsive to insulin, raising the risk of Type 2 diabetes (1)
extra weight strains joints and the heart (1)
markScheme.guidance: 3 marks for a full explanation; 2 marks for a partial explanation; 1 mark for a limited explanation
